charles-davis-upper-marlboro-1915-08-12.A1:
HELD AS A HORSE THIEF.
Charles Davis, Washington Negro, in Jail at Upper Marlboro. Special Correspondence of The Star
Special Correspondence of The Star.

UPPER MARLBORO, Md., August 12.—Charles Davis, colored, a resident of Washington, was lodged in jail here last night to answer charges of horse stealing. He was arrested by Sheriff Hardy as a result of the investigation of the disappearance of two horses from this section of the county in May. The prisoner denies the charge, but, it is stated, admits he had possession of one of the horses in question, claiming he purchased it from "John Brown of Richmond."

Benjamin Bowie's horse was taken May 9, and sold in Washington for $10. It was recovered yesterday. A horse that belonged to Bruce Buck was stolen May 17, taken to Washington and worked. Last week it was sold for $5, the purchaser paying $2.80 on account, and it was in such a miserable condition that a policeman killed it. Its carcass was identified by Mr. Buck.

Davis returned to the county yesterday and was arrested. He may have a hearing tomorrow.
charles-davis-upper-marlboro-1915-08-12.A2:
WITHDRAW GUARDS
AT MARLBORO JAIL
Sheriff Hardy Explains That Extra Men Was Simply Precaution Against Violence.
With no further fears that a lynching will be attempted at the Marlboro jail, where Charles Davis, colored, charged with horse stealing, is confined, Sheriff Hardy announced today that the armed guard which surrounded the jail last night for Davis' protection was withdrawn.

"There was no demonstration against Davis," Sheriff Hardy explained, "and our only reason for placing the guard about the jail last evening was the report that reached us that violence might be attempted. We placde the guard there to be on the safe side."

It was learned today that the lynching talk came from a group under the influence of liquor and that there had been no general movement to attempt to break into the jail for Davis.

Davis, who formerly lived in Washington, is charged with stealing a horse valued at $250 from the farm of Bruce Buck, near Upper Marlboro, on May 27 last. His alleged treatment of the horse rather than the stealing was the cause of the indignation against him Wednesday night.

Davis is said to have kept the horse since May, almost without food, and on Saturday, when it was nearly dead from hunger, and in an emaciated condition, to have sold it to a man in Washington who had to shoot the horse the next day.

The horse was found by Detective Springman at the crematory near Brightwood. The arrest of Davis followed.

Davis is also charged with stealing a horse valued at $150 from the farm of Benjamin H. C. Bowie, near Bowie, Md. This animal he is charged with having sold to a man on Milk Ford road, Brightwood, D. C., for $10. This horse has been recovered and returned to its owner.

GUARDS AGAINST LYNCHING.
Marlboro Sheriff Protects Colored
Man Accused of Horse Stealing.
UPPER MARLBORO, August 13.—Two guards were on duty in the county jail last night to protect Charles Davis, colored, alleged horse thief. Sheriff Hardy was told of a report that a lynching had been talked of because of the bad treatment to which the prisoner was said to have subjected a horse that belonged to Bruce Buck, a resident of Queen Anne district.

The animal died in Washington, it is stated, from ill treatment and starvation. Sheriff Hardy heard that the talk about lynching was started by a man who probably had been imbibing too freely, and, although he did not believe there was any danger, he took precautions.

Davis will be arraigned before Justice of the Peace J. Alfred Ridgley Tuesday for a preliminary hearing. He denies the charge. It is probable that witnesses will be brought from Washington to testify against the prisoner.
charles-davis-upper-marlboro-1915-08-12.A4:
Charles Davis Arrested as the Horse Thief.
Charles Davis, colored, was arrested and placed in jail on Monday evening on suspicion of being the thief who stole the horses belonging to Mr. Benj. Bowie and Mr. Bruce Buck several months ago.

Davis walked into town on Monday evening and was recognized by several persons as the stranger who was seen in the neighborhood on the days the horses were stolen.

He was questioned in jail by States Attorney Roberts and Sheriff Hardy and from information gained they found that he lived in Montgomery county, near Tenleytown, and was a huckster. From his neighbors, the Sheriff and Mr. Buck learned that Davis had had two horses tallying with the stolen horses and Mr. Bowie's horse was found working in a contractor's wagon in Tenleytown, to whom Davis had sold him for $10. The other horse which resembled the stolen horse of Mr. Buck's had been worked and starved by Davis until on Monday morning he fell in the street. Davis then sold him lying down to a man for $5.00, and before this man could get him up a policeman came along and shot the horse. The hide of this horse was found, but it was so badly scarred that identification was difficult. It is said Davis left his wagon and harness with the man to whom he sold the last horse and told him he would be back the next day after it. He was seen by several people Monday afternoon walking the road to Marlboro from Oak Grove, with a package under his arm and when arrested a few hours afterward he had no package. This package, it is believed contained a bridle and was hidden by him on the rood side until night when he would get another horse.

Much sympathy is felt for Mr. Buck who not only lost one of the most valuable horses of the neighborhood but has spent a great deal of time and money in trying to locate him since he was stolen.

If Davis is guilty it is to be hoped that he will be convicted and punished severely.

john-riggins-bainbridge-1915-08-17.A11:
NEGRO IS LYNCHED
IN DECATUR COUNTY
Attacks White Woman as She Drives Along Country Road. Victim Identifies Her Assailant.
BAINBRIDGE, Ga.—So far as is known the first criminal assault in the history of Decatur county occurred Monday afternoon between Amsterdam and Attapulgus. A promo of the tobacco men there, was the victim.

She was driving along a country road when the negro sprang into the buggy and overpowered her. Searching parties early last night captured the assailant, and after carrying him before the victim she identified him after saving the lives of several others during the day through failure to accuse them.

The negro's victim has been unconscious much of the time since the assault, and although she was already in delicate health is reported to be resting well.

AUGUSTA (GA) WEEKLY LETTER Cupid's arrow.
Georgia's shame has been further accelerated through the lynching of Leo. M. Frank and a colored man at Bainbridge this week. The lynching of Negroes is so common that the case at Bainbridge received only passing notice, but the great commotion results in the case of Frank. Frank had been convicted of assaulting and murdering a white girl who was employed by him in a pencil factory in Atlanta, the crime, was an atrocious one and many of the details of it were too revolting for publication. He was able to marshal a slush fund of the emergency size, and after a fight thru all the courts of the state and the United States Supreme Court, all of which decided against him, then Governor Slaton came to his rescue and commuted him to penitentiary for life. There appears no doubt that Frank ravished and then murdered the poor girl and the people of the state were sure of his guilt and resented bitterly the action of Governor Slaton in undoing the work of the courts. Their feeling was fanned into a flame which finally enveloped the state farm where Frank was confined, and from which he was taken to his death at a point two miles from the grave of his victim, near Marietta. To-day some prominent people are pawing the earth over this lynching and demanding that the members of the mob be brought to book.

The contrast between the case of Frank and the lynching of the Negro at Bainbridge on the same day is painful. The Governor is to offer the limit in rewards for the lynching of Frank while not one dollar is to be offered for the apprehension and punishment of the mob which lynched the Negro. He was simply charged with assault and had not had a trial which could have established either his innocence or guilt. Our laws may be all right as to their letter, but some of the high officials seem fearfully warped as to their enforcement. All good citizens must deplore these lynchings, and it is hoped that out of them may come a more wholesome respect for law and regard for human life—whether a black man or a white man be involved.

A LETTER FROM GEORGIA.
Editor The Leader: I am a subscriber to The Milwaukee Leader and have been since the first issue was published. I would positively cut out enough food bill to save the price of The Leader before I would do without it.

Now, listen! in regard to the Leo M. Frank case. I am a Georgian by birth, live in Georgia, and am all over Georgia. And I just want to tell you that 90 per cent of the population of Georgia approve of the disposition of this case. Now, if you print what you believe, and believe what you print, get the facts in this case.

If you want the whole truth, and I believe you do, write Thomas E. Watson, Thomson, Ga., and you will get them exactly as they exist—a matter of the records, pure facts and not heresy. He can prove to your satisfaction that John M. Slaton, who rode rough shod over all the courts in our land, and over the sentiment of 90 per cent of the people of Georgia, to commute Frank's sentence, was a partner to the law firm that represented Frank. It is the opinion of a big majority of the best people of Georgia that John M. Slaton played the part of a Benedict Arnold. Just after this act of treason, Slaton left Georgia, and has not returned. Many Georgians believe that he has no intentions of ever putting his foot on Georgia soil again.

I live at Bainbridge, in the southwestern part of the state. A few days ago, at Amsterdam, just 14 miles from our town, a negro was lynched for assaulting a northern woman. When he was caught, he confessed to the crime, and was executed immediately. So you see Georgia protects the virtue of her women, regardless of the race, the color, the nationality, or the station in life of the aggressor.

The views of that doctor open up a wide vista for speculation. The philosophy behind them applies not to food alone, but to all human relations. We speak as if liking and disliking were beyond our control. They usually are. But the reason is that we have allowed them to get beyond our control. We have made them an habitual form of self-indulgence, exactly as De Pachmann did in the matter of yellow flowers.

If, years ago, De Pachmann had made up his mind that he would derive, not pain, but pleasure, from yellow flowers, he could have ridden himself of a cause of irritation and acquired another source of pleasure. Incidentally he would have strengthened his capacity for liking.

As a matter of fact, if we could look into De Pachmann's mind we should find that the prejudice was only one of many prejudices, all expressing a weak tendency to yield to passing ill-humor.

There are certain lines that people who are given to disliking often quote:

"I do not like you, Doctor Fell,
The reason why I can not tell."

It's a great pity these lines were ever written. They became popular because they seemed to offer a justification for disliking, an exceedingly silly justification.

As a matter of fact, disliking has no real justification. It is a pure waste. The things that inspire dislike ought not to be thought of at all. The really healthy mind turns away from them. It busies itself, not with negotiations, but with positives, with things that appeal to sympathy and interest, that enrich and broaden character and life.

It is pitiful at times to hear people talk about their dislikes. The weakness is commoner among women than among men. For among men there has grown up a half-conscious feeling that repeated expressions of dislike are petty and therefore unmanly. It is seldom that one hears a man speak with pride of his dislikes. He is more likely to be a little ashamed of them and to keep them out of sight. But women, who specialize in disliking, speak as if their dislikes reflected only the character of the objects disliked, forgetting the reactionary influence on themselves, and the revelation of their own habits of feeling and thinking and criticizing.

The more we dislike the more dislike we create in others through the resentment, we create. Even inanimate things seem to be controlled by this law and take on a kind of life presenting to us their more hateful aspects.

On the other hand, by liking we achieve results exactly opposite. We find more things and more people and incidentally, we find that we are ourselves more liked and more likable.

FIGURES.

Editor The Leader: Here's a figure coincidence: Take two years of the Franco-German war and add them together:

1870+1871=3741.

The figures thus obtained give you the duration of the war, for it began on the third day of the seventh month of 1870 and ended on the fourth of the first month of 1871. Then add the two years of the present war:

1914+1915=3829.

Sure enough, the war did commence on the third day of the eighth month of 1914.

If the thing works out right, the war should be ended on the second of the ninth month of this year.

Here's hoping it does.

IRVIN ZOLINSKY.

Posse After Negro.
[United Press Leased Wire Service.]
KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 6.—A posse with blood hounds was believed at noon to be close upon the trail of a negro who attacked the wife of Ned Stafford at her home near Liberty yesterday. The dogs kept the trail all night, closely followed by enraged farmers.

The husband of the victim, with a shot gun, is the first man behind the hounds and is commanding the man hunt. The black's life will be worth little if the crowd overtakes him. The dogs are headed for Kansas City.
mrs-henry-stafford-liberty-1915-08-05.A4:
ARMED MEN PURSUE NEGRO.
Posse of 500 Searching for Assailant of White Woman.
KANSAS CITY, Mo., August 6.—A section seven miles square in the southwest corner of Clay county, across the Missouri river north from here, is surrounded by 500 armed men today searching for the negro who yesterday attacked Mrs. Henry Stafford, wife of a young farmer near Liberty, Mo.

The posses have followed the negro's trail from the Stafford home into the wooded hills of the southwest corner of the county, and the leaders believe he had had no opportunity to escape from the district surrounded.

Mrs. Stafford was said to be in a dangerous condition today.
mrs-henry-stafford-liberty-1915-08-05.A10:
Women See Executions and Crowd Sings Hymn-One Slayer Pursued.
MEMPHIS, Aug. 7.—Nine negroes were hanged, seven legally and two lynched, yesterday, in the southern states, while a tenth is being chased near Liberty, Mo., by a lynching party.

Alabama led the list with four legal hangings. The governor refused reprieves in each case. At Evergreen, Robert Watkins and John Salter were hanged while a squad of militiamen stood guard to prevent disorder, threatened by citizens who wanted the blacks burned for the murder and assault of Mrs. Mary Lassiter at Cullman.

George James was hanged for the murder of George Clayburn, who was shot through an open window while he was reading a Bible. Millard Carpenter was hanged at Birmingham for the murder two years ago of John T. Camp, a white man.

WOMEN ATTEND HANGING.

Mississippi hanged three negroes, but with two of them, Peter Bolen and Jim Seales, convicted of murdering another negro, an unusual spectacle was made. The hanging was at Fresco, the gallows being erected between two beautiful hills in a natural amphitheater.

Many women were in the crowd of 5,000 people and excursions were run from nearby towns. Just as the traps were sprung simultaneously the crowd burst forth into the hymn, "There Is a Land of Pure Delight," at the request of the negroes just before death.

Bunyan Walters was hanged at Fayetteville, Miss., for the murder of Tom Neals.

AN "ORDERLY MOB."

Dispatches from Shawnee, Okla., tell of a "quiet, orderly crowd armed to the teeth," which hanged Ed Berry to a Santa Fe railroad bridge, riddled his body with bullets and dispersed in as orderly a fashion as it had formed.

In the early morning hours at Trilby, Fla., a crowd, hypnotized with fury, lynched Will Leach, accused of attacking a 13-year-old girl.

At last reports a mob of 500 men were closing in on a negro near Liberty, Mo., who attacked a farmer's wife. Lynching is almost certain, it is said.

POSSE CONTINUES SEARCH
Hundreds on Trail of Negro Assailant of White Woman.
KANSAS CITY, MO., August 2. — Hope of capturing the negro who yesterday attacked Mrs. Henry Stafford, wife of a young farmer, in her home near Liberty, Mo., was not abandoned to-night by the posse of several hundred men who had trailed the negro over the wooded hills of Clay County for more than twenty-four hours.

Late to-day the bloodhounds, which had pointed out the negro's tracks all night and to-day, lost the trail. They were exhausted from the negro the long hunt, and refused to continue.

The officers were confident the negro had not escaped from the territory formed by the Missouri River and the lines of men. These lines will be maintained through the night, and a patrol placed along the river bank.

RAIN STOPS MAN HUNT IN
CLAY COUNTY MISSOURI
KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 7.—Rain today ended the search for the negro who Thursday afternoon attacked Mrs. Henry Stafford, wife of a young farmer living near Liberty, Mo. A posse, numbering at one time 500 men, surrounded the southwestern corner of Clay county two hours after Mrs. Stafford was discovered tied to a bed in her home, and the entire territory inside the posse's lines was combed several times without avail. Althuogh the bloodhounds lost the trail of the negro late yesterday, the searchers did not despair of his capture until rain drove them in today.
mrs-henry-stafford-liberty-1915-08-05.A27:
Negro Attacks Clay County Woman.
Liberty, Mo., Aug. 6.—Mrs. Henry Stafford, wife of a farmer living four miles north of Liberty, was brutally attacked by a negro in her home yesterday morning. She was in the house alone with her baby, her mother-in-law having gone to a mail box. The negro entered the house overpowered and gagged her, tossing the infant into a cradle in an adjoining room. After the attack she was bound to the bed, where she was found in an unconscious condition later. While her condition is serious physicians say she will recover. Mr. Stafford was away from home with a threshing crew when the attack occurred. The news of the assault spread rapidly over the neighborhood. Threshing crews stopped work, farmers left their tasks and in a short while at least 100 men and boys were in the field with weapons of all kind bent on avenging the crime.

Missouri Posse Hunts Negro. Kansas City, Mo., Aug. 9.—News that Mrs. Henry Stafford, who was attacked by a negro at her home near Liberty, Mo., had suffered a nervous breakdown and was dangerously ill, stirred the citizens of Southern Clay county to renew the hunt for her assailant. A fresh pack of blood-hounds replaced those which, after following the trail a night and a day, abandoned it because of fatigue. Almost $100,000 in rewards for the capture of the negro, dead or alive, have been raised.

thomas-collins-bunkie.A2:
The special session of the grand jury, called by Judge Lafargue, to investigate the recent lynching of a negro in Bunkie County, completed its investigations and made a report of its findings to the court. The report of the grand jury declared that the body failed to secure sufficient evidence to hold any person responsible for the lynching.

Mayor F. E. Girard of Lafayette stated that he is well pleased with the operation of the "curfew law" which has been in effect for several weeks and which the police have had little trouble to enforce. The ordinance requires all children under sixteen years of age to be off the streets by nine o'clock at night unless accompanied by guardians.
thomas-collins-bunkie.A4: Thomas Collins, a negro at Bunkle, La., accused of wounding a policeman, was hanged by a mob.
